owner_posts.post_text:
Self-Esteem and Identity Therapy

Low self-esteem can affect far more than confidence. It can shape your decisions, relationships, ambitions, self-expression, and the way you speak to yourself every day. You may struggle with self-doubt, shame, insecurity, harsh self-criticism, body image concerns, or a deeper confusion about who you are and what you really want. In therapy, I do not offer surface-level confidence advice. I help you understand how these patterns developed, why they keep repeating, and what may be needed for real change. My style is reflective, depth-oriented, and emotionally engaged. Therapy can help you build a more stable sense of self, reduce self-attack, trust your own mind more, make clearer decisions, and begin living with greater confidence, authenticity, and self-respect.

Trauma Therapy

Trauma can continue affecting you long after the painful event is over. It may show up as fear, emotional overwhelm, numbness, mistrust, shame, panic, relationship difficulties, or feeling that the past is still shaping how you respond in the present. Sometimes people do not even think of their experience as trauma, but they know something in them still feels unsettled, guarded, or deeply hurt. In therapy, I work in a paced, respectful, and emotionally containing way. My approach is depth-oriented and sensitive to both emotional safety and the deeper impact of painful experiences. The aim is not to force you to relive what happened, but to help you process it, understand its effects, reduce its hold on your life, and gradually build a stronger sense of safety, stability, and emotional freedom.

Overthinking and OCD Therapy

Overthinking and OCD can leave you feeling trapped inside your own mind. You may keep replaying things, doubting yourself, checking, analysing, seeking reassurance, or struggling with intrusive thoughts that feel upsetting, confusing, or hard to control. These patterns can take away peace of mind, drain energy, and make even simple decisions feel exhausting. In therapy, I work with both the distress you are facing and the deeper emotional patterns that may be keeping these cycles active. My style is careful, non-judgmental, and psychologically in-depth, while still practical enough to help you respond differently in daily life. Therapy can help you reduce the grip of obsessive thinking, feel less controlled by fear and doubt, and regain a greater sense of freedom, clarity, and trust in yourself.

Depression Therapy

Depression is not always obvious from the outside. Sometimes it looks like low mood, tiredness, emptiness, irritability, loss of interest, emotional numbness, crying spells, or simply feeling stuck in survival mode. It can affect motivation, sleep, work, relationships, and your sense of meaning in life. In therapy, I offer a space where your suffering is taken seriously and explored with care. My approach is thoughtful, emotionally attentive, and depth-oriented, with focus on both what is happening now and what may be shaping it underneath. Therapy can help you understand what is weighing you down, reduce self-criticism, reconnect with yourself, and slowly begin to feel more alive, more hopeful, and more able to engage with life again in a meaningful way.

Anxiety Therapy

Anxiety can make daily life feel heavy, tense, and difficult to switch off from. You may find yourself constantly worrying, overthinking, feeling restless, panicky, physically on edge, or expecting something to go wrong even when things seem fine on the surface. Over time, anxiety can affect sleep, work, relationships, confidence, and your ability to feel settled in yourself. In therapy, I help you understand not only the symptoms, but also the emotional patterns and pressures that may be driving them. My style is calm, thoughtful, and depth-oriented, while still practical and grounded. The aim is not just temporary relief, but a deeper sense of steadiness, better emotional regulation, clearer thinking, and the ability to face life with more confidence and less fear.

Anger and Emotional Regulation Therapy

Anger often carries more beneath it than people realise. It may involve frustration, hurt, resentment, helplessness, shame, or feeling repeatedly misunderstood and overwhelmed. When anger shows up as irritability, harsh tone, emotional outbursts, jealousy, impulsive reactions, or difficulty calming down, it can damage relationships, create tension at work or home, and leave you feeling guilty afterward. In therapy, I help you understand not just the anger itself, but what happens inside you before it escalates. My style is direct, thoughtful, and emotionally focused, without being shaming or moralistic. Therapy can help you become less reactive, regulate emotions better, communicate more clearly, and respond with more control, maturity, and steadiness in difficult situations.

Some messages stay with you. 🌿

A young student I supported during her board exam phase recently wrote to share that she scored 98 and felt that our work together helped her stay calmer, steadier, and able to function well under pressure.

Moments like these are deeply meaningful. Academic performance is never only about intelligence or effort; emotional containment, clarity, and psychological support can make a real difference when it matters most.

Grateful to be trusted in such important phases of people’s lives.

featured_reviews.name: RAM MALKANI
featured_reviews.review_text:
I started therapy with Dr. Tejas Shah during the COVID period in 2020, when I was in a very difficult mental state. Living near Worli sea face, constantly hearing ambulance sirens, reading about COVID, and knowing that older people and those with heart problems were more vulnerable made me extremely anxious. I stopped going out, lost 12 kg, stopped working, and gradually slipped into mild depression. Even basic daily routines became difficult.

Although I was advised to take antidepressants, I was not in favor of psychotropic medication. On the recommendation of my psychologist, I began talk therapy with Dr. Tejas Shah—initially twice a week, and later up to five times a week.

Over time, therapy helped me not only with the fear and distress of that period, but also with long-standing issues of self-doubt, self-criticism, lack of confidence, and feeling “not good enough.” Since 2024, I have gradually reduced therapy to twice a week, which I continue till now (April 2026).

Today, I feel much more relaxed, less self-critical, and more socially at ease. I enjoy conversations, feel more spontaneous, and am much less shy than before. I also see the difference in my professional work. I am calmer with patients, more attentive, and more confident in explaining medical as well as psychological aspects of their condition. I feel I am maturing into a better Psycho-Dermatologist.

At the age of 80, I continue to work, pursue my PhD, journal daily, and stay mentally active. I still have some challenges, such as anxiety before presentations, but I can clearly see how much progress I have made.

I find Dr. Tejas Shah to be a very good analyst—patient, attentive, and a deeply thoughtful listener. His integrative therapy approach has helped bring about meaningful change in my life. I intend to continue therapy with him, now twice a week, for as long as my mind permits.

featured_reviews.review_text:
I took up therapy with Tejas when I was at the lowest point of my life.

Facing severe anxiety, I went into therapy having absolutely no clue of what to expect.

And Tejas helped pull me out of the depths of depression, slowly but surely.

Tejas’ working style is reassuring — he treads softly and humanely, making sure that the patient does not feel uncomfortable during the therapy process.

Initially, I had a feeling that he does not speak much and wondered if that was not a good thing.

But I realised that when he does speak, his observations give you plenty of food for thought, and his subtle nudges can bring about a vast change in the way you see and process things.

I did therapy with him for two years, at the end of which I emerged much more emotionally aware than I was when I started. The impact of the changes I was able to bring about manifests itself everyday in my life — and it feels great to notice how differently you respond to situations now.

If there is one thing I would pick on with my experience - I found the therapy structure rigid. In that, I found no room for making any changes to the timings, etc, and you couldn’t speak much with him outside of therapy hours. I would put that down to his busy working schedule but on the odd occasion, I could not shake the feeling that he should have been more available emotionally.

On the whole, it is not an overstatement for me to say Tejas changed my life. I shudder to think where I would have been today if I hadn’t taken up therapy in general, and therapy with Tejas in particular.

If you’re considering therapy, working with Tejas is a decision you will not regret.

owner_posts.post_text: In a world that’s always ‘on,’ the real strength today is knowing when to pause. Feeling mentally drained doesn’t mean you’re failing — it means you’ve been carrying too much for too long. Give yourself permission to rest, unplug, and breathe. Protecting your peace is productivity too.

Summer can affect mental health in different ways. For some people, sunshine and longer days may improve mood. For others, rising temperatures can worsen anxiety, low mood, irritability, fatigue, and poor sleep.

Heat places extra stress on the body, can disturb sleep, and may intensify physical sensations like a racing heart or restlessness, which can feel similar to anxiety. Poor sleep during warmer nights can also affect concentration, emotional balance, and energy levels.

At the same time, simple protective habits can make a real difference: staying hydrated, keeping a regular routine, gentle movement, rest, and spending time in calming natural spaces.

In simple terms: summer can boost mood when the body is well-regulated. Prioritising sleep, hydration, and rest is not just self-care~it is mental health care.

We at Mindsight encourage you to stay hydrated, slow down when needed, and take gentle care of your mind and body this summer. ☀️

Resilience check-in 🌱

We often think resilient people have it all together… but the truth is, they feel overwhelmed too.

Resilience isn’t about avoiding hard moments – it’s about how we move through them, in our own time and in our own way.

Self-Discipline vs Self-Compassion: 

Which one actually helps you stay consistent?

We’re often taught that strict self-discipline and self-criticism are the keys to success. 

But research and clinical experience show that self-compassion—being kind, understanding, and realistic with yourself—actually leads to better consistency over time. 

When you respond to mistakes with curiosity instead of harsh judgment, you reduce shame, build emotional safety, and make it easier to try again.

Self-discipline rooted in self-compassion isn’t about “letting yourself off the hook”; it’s about supporting yourself in a way that makes growth sustainable, not exhausting. 🌱

Square Breathing (Box Breathing): A Simple Technique for Panic Attacks

When anxiety or panic starts to rise, square breathing can help slow your breathing and calm your body’s stress response.

⬜ Step 1: Breathe in through your nose for 4 seconds
⬜ Step 2: Hold your breath for 4 seconds
⬜ Step 3: Breathe out slowly through your mouth for 4 seconds
⬜ Step 4: Hold your breath again for 4 seconds

Repeat this cycle for 1–3 minutes or until you feel calmer.

Why it helps:
During a panic attack, breathing often becomes rapid and shallow. Square breathing encourages slow, controlled breaths, which can reduce physical symptoms such as a racing heart, dizziness, and feelings of panic.

Hidden Symptoms of Anxiety: More Than Just Worry

Anxiety doesn't always look like panic attacks or visible nervousness. Often, it shows up through subtle emotional, physical, and behavioral symptoms that can easily be overlooked or mistaken for everyday stress.

🔹 Overthinking: Constantly analyzing situations, worrying about the future, or replaying past events can be a sign of underlying anxiety.

🔹 Poor Sleep: Difficulty falling asleep, frequent waking during the night, or waking up feeling unrested may be linked to an anxious mind.

🔹 Headaches: Persistent tension headaches or unexplained physical discomfort can sometimes be caused by chronic stress and anxiety.

🔹 Fatigue: Living in a constant state of worry can be mentally and physically exhausting, leading to low energy levels even after adequate rest.

🔹 Irritability: Increased frustration, impatience, or emotional sensitivity may be an indication that anxiety is affecting your daily life.

Ignoring these symptoms can impact your relationships, work performance, and overall quality of life. The good news is that anxiety is treatable, and with the right support, individuals can regain control, improve emotional well-being, and lead healthier, more balanced lives.

At Dr. Yeshwant Solanki Psychiatry Clinic, we help individuals identify the root causes of anxiety and provide personalized treatment and support to promote long-term mental wellness.

If these symptoms sound familiar, seeking help is a sign of strength

What Happens in the Brain During a Panic Attack?

A panic attack can feel sudden, intense, and overwhelming. Many people describe it as feeling like they are losing control, having a heart attack, or facing immediate danger. While these experiences are frightening, they are often the result of the brain's natural survival system becoming overactive.

🔹 Fight-or-Flight Mode Activates
The brain mistakenly interprets a situation as threatening, triggering the body's emergency response system.

🔹 Overactive Amygdala
The amygdala, the brain's fear center, becomes highly active and sends signals that something is wrong—even when there is no real danger present.

🔹 Stress Hormones Increase
Adrenaline and cortisol are released into the bloodstream, preparing the body to react quickly to a perceived threat.

🔹 Fast Heartbeat
The heart pumps faster to send more oxygen-rich blood to the muscles, which can cause palpitations or chest discomfort.

🔹 Rapid Breathing
Breathing becomes quicker and shallower, sometimes leading to dizziness, tingling sensations, or a feeling of breathlessness.

🔹 Clouded Thinking
The brain focuses on survival rather than rational thinking, making it difficult to concentrate, think clearly, or feel in control.

🔹 Intense Fear
A powerful sense of fear, panic, or impending doom may occur, even when there is no obvious reason for the reaction.

🔹 High Alert State
The body remains hypervigilant, scanning for danger and making it difficult to relax.

Success & Depression: The Hidden Struggle Behind Achievement

Success is often seen as the ultimate goal, but for many high achievers, it can come with unexpected emotional challenges. Behind professional accomplishments, financial stability, and recognition, there may be feelings of pressure, exhaustion, stress, and emotional imbalance.

🔹 High Pressure: Constant expectations to perform and maintain success can create overwhelming mental strain.

🔹 Emotional Exhaustion: Continuous responsibilities and the need to stay productive can lead to burnout, leaving individuals feeling drained and disconnected.

🔹 Constant Stress: Managing work, family, finances, and personal goals simultaneously can affect mental and emotional well-being.

🔹 Lack of Balance: Prioritizing achievement over self-care may impact relationships, health, and overall happiness.

Success should not come at the cost of mental health. Recognizing the signs of stress, burnout, anxiety, or depression is the first step toward recovery and emotional well-being. Seeking professional support can help individuals develop healthier coping strategies, restore balance, and lead a more fulfilling life.

At Dr. Yeshwant Solanki Psychiatry Clinic, we believe that mental wellness is just as important as professional success. If you or someone you know is struggling despite outward achievements, help is available.

Your success matters—but so does your mental health.

5 Signs Your Anxiety Is More Than Just Stress

Feeling stressed from time to time is a normal part of life. However, when worry, fear, or nervousness starts affecting your daily routine, it may be a sign of anxiety that needs professional attention. Anxiety disorders are common and treatable, but many people ignore the early warning signs.

Here are five signs that your anxiety may be more than just everyday stress:

✔ Constant Overthinking – Repeatedly worrying about situations, conversations, or future events can make it difficult to relax and enjoy daily life.

✔ Trouble Sleeping – Difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up feeling tired may be linked to ongoing anxiety.

✔ Feeling Restless Often – Constant nervousness, irritability, or an inability to sit still can indicate heightened anxiety levels.

✔ Difficulty Concentrating – Anxiety can make it hard to focus on work, studies, or even simple daily tasks.

✔ Physical Symptoms – Anxiety may also cause headaches, fatigue, rapid heartbeat, muscle tension, or digestive issues.

If these symptoms persist for weeks or begin interfering with your personal, social, or professional life, seeking help from a mental health professional can make a significant difference. Early diagnosis and proper treatment can help you regain control, improve emotional well-being, and enhance your quality of life.

Dr. Yeshwant Solanki, Psychiatrist, provides compassionate and evidence-based care for anxiety, stress-related disorders

Are You Overthinking or Problem Solving?

It is natural for the mind to analyze situations and seek solutions, but there is a fine line between healthy problem solving and unproductive overthinking. Understanding this difference is essential for maintaining mental clarity and emotional well-being.

Problem solving is a constructive process. It involves identifying an issue, evaluating possible solutions, and taking actionable steps toward resolution. It is goal-oriented, time-bound, and helps individuals move forward with confidence and clarity.

On the other hand, overthinking is repetitive and often unproductive. It involves dwelling on the same thoughts, worrying about possibilities, and replaying situations without reaching a clear outcome. This pattern can lead to increased anxiety, stress, and mental fatigue, making it harder to make decisions or take action.

Overthinking often creates confusion and self-doubt, while problem solving empowers individuals to feel in control and focused. Recognizing when your thoughts are becoming circular rather than solution-focused is the first step toward change.

With the right guidance, individuals can learn to shift from overthinking to effective problem solving through structured thinking, mindfulness, and cognitive strategies. Seeking professional support can further help in developing healthier thought patterns and improving overall mental well-being.

— Dr. Yeshwant Solanki

Panic Attack Symptoms

Panic attacks are sudden episodes of intense fear or discomfort that can occur without warning and may feel overwhelming. They often mimic serious physical health conditions, which can make them particularly distressing for individuals experiencing them for the first time.

One of the most common symptoms is a rapid heartbeat, where the heart feels like it is racing or pounding uncontrollably. This is often accompanied by shortness of breath, making it difficult to breathe normally and creating a sensation of suffocation.

Many individuals also experience chest pain or discomfort, which can be alarming and sometimes mistaken for a cardiac issue. Alongside this, excessive sweating may occur, even in calm or cool environments, as the body responds to heightened anxiety.

Other symptoms include dizziness or lightheadedness, which can make a person feel unsteady or disconnected from their surroundings, and nausea or stomach discomfort, adding to the overall sense of unease.

Recognizing these symptoms is important for early identification and management of panic attacks. With proper psychological support, coping strategies, and professional guidance, individuals can learn to manage these episodes effectively and regain a sense of control.

— Dr. Yeshwant Solanki
